title: Three ways of saying a short vowel that counts as long

slides.heading: No new letters, and three arrivals on the steps
body: No new consonant. Every word today is built from letters you have.
Three vowels, all of them at the front steps.
Short in the mouth, counted long for the tone.
A repeat mark, and two consonants run together.

slides.heading: Pen and paper
body: Real paper, a real pen.
Both halves of the name, out loud, every time.

slides.heading: The busiest room in the house
body: The steps opened in lesson seven and have been filling ever since.
Three more lodgers arrive today.
Written ahead of the consonant, spoken after it.

slides.heading: The first one comes in two pieces
body: A mast in front, the consonant, then the long post from lesson one.
One vowel written in two pieces, in two rooms.
The sound is the vowel in *how*, and it goes by fast.

slides.heading: Write it
body: Mast, then consonant, then the long post. In that order on the page.
Say it aloud with the consonant leaving your mouth first.
Put the boat's letter in the middle and try it.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: The mast, the boat's letter, the long post.
One vowel wrapped round one consonant. Out loud before you turn it over.

slides.heading: That one
body: **เรา** — we, or us.
Also a very common everyday word for *I*.

slides.heading: The second one, and the common one
body: A single mast with a zigzag broken into its top.
The sound is the English word *I*, said fast.
This is the ordinary spelling, and you will meet it constantly.

slides.heading: Write it
body: One upright with a sharp zigzag on top.
Write it ahead of the fish's letter and say it aloud.
Consonant out of the mouth first, then the vowel.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: The zigzag mast, then the fish's letter.
Out loud before you turn it over.

slides.heading: That one
body: **ไป** — to go.
The 34th commonest word in the language.

slides.heading: The third one, which sounds exactly like the second
body: A single mast with its top rolled into a curl.
The same sound as the zigzag, with nothing in the sound to separate them.
The word's spelling decides which one it takes.

slides.heading: Write it
body: One upright with a rolled curl on top.
Write it beside the zigzag and compare the two tops.
A flick against a curl. Nothing else separates them.

slides.heading: Which words take the curl
body: **ใน** — in. The 23rd commonest word in Thai.
**ใจ** — the heart, or the mind.
**ใบ** — a leaf.
**ใด** — any.

slides.prompt: You hear a Thai word with this sound in it and you have to write it down. Which of the two spellings do you reach for, and how confident should you be?

answers: Reach for the zigzag **ไ**, unless you know the word is on the list.
The curl **ใ** covers roughly twenty words, and the zigzag covers everything else.
Learn the twenty as words, one at a time, as you meet them.

slides.heading: Short in the mouth, long for the tone
body: The three vowels today are genuinely short in the mouth.
For working out a tone, all three are counted long.
A syllable ending on one of them is live.

slides.heading: What the live and dead rule is actually measuring
body: **Dead** means something at the back stopped the air.
**ไป** ends on its vowel, with nothing behind it to stop anything.
**ตก** stops on the chicken's letter, and the air goes nowhere.
What stops the syllable is the whole of what the rule measures.

slides.prompt: ไป is over as fast as any short vowel you know. Say why it still takes the live rule rather than the dead one.

answers: Nothing stops it, so the syllable is live.
Put a stopping consonant behind the vowel and it becomes dead.
**ไป** opens on a market letter and ends live, so lesson three's rule settles it.

slides.heading: The mark that means say it twice
body: Punctuation rather than a letter, and no sound of its own.
It stands after a word and tells you to say that word again.
A space is left in front of it.

slides.heading: What doubling a word actually does
body: **เด็ก ๆ** — children, from the word for a child.
English doubling usually intensifies.
Thai doubling usually broadens, and makes the word less exact.

slides.heading: Two consonants that run together into one sound
body: Two consonants can also run straight together into one sound.
One syllable, with the two letters sharing a single onset.
Only three letters can stand second, and the rule names all three.
Last lesson gave you the other reading of two bare consonants.

slides.heading: Read this one
body: The curled mast, the buffalo's letter, the boat's letter.
The last two run together into a single syllable.
Out loud before you turn it over.

slides.heading: That one
body: **ใคร** — who, and a fifth word taking the curl.
**ใคร ๆ** — anyone at all.

slides.heading: One more, and you have been waiting for it
body: The zigzag mast, the soldier's letter, the giant's letter.
Out loud before you turn it over.

slides.heading: That one
body: **ไทย** — Thai, and Thailand.
The last piece it needed was today's zigzag mast.

slides.heading: Words you can read with them
body: **ไฟ** — fire.
**เอา** — to take, or to want. The ring at its front is silent.
**ดีใจ** — glad. Good, and a heart.
**ตกใจ** — frightened. A heart that falls.

slides.heading: Twenty letters, eighteen vowels
body: Eighteen vowel spellings, and no new letters today.
A vowel at the back of a syllable stops nothing, so the syllable is live.
Next: the letter from lesson six gets its name, and the market's grid closes.
